## AGENTS.md
SHA-256: 9adff6744cc0649465d77314f3d3697627029438963e4cede9a3b1546d0bbcc6
~~~text
    1 | # Pocket Rivals — universal rules
    2 | 
    3 | - Work inside this project; the surrounding grading workspace is unrelated. Preserve the existing visual identity.
    4 | - TypeScript strict, Phaser 3, Vite, Capacitor. One Phaser instance and render loop. No backend, ads, analytics, accounts, remote assets or AI services.
    5 | - Read `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, the contract and the target module's AGENTS.md. Do not read or modify unrelated games by default.
    6 | - Modules live in `src/games/*` or `src/arcade/*`. Only lightweight config/thumbnail metadata is eager. Factories, rules, physics and AI load on demand. Never import one game into another or into core/shared.
    7 | - Keep factories/constructors free of listeners and side effects. Initialize with GameContext; own and dispose every scene resource, worker, timer and subscription. Host-owned input is cleared on pause and disposed on shutdown.
    8 | - Simulations use fixed/bounded steps. Match clocks use foreground monotonic elapsed time. Preserve pointer identity, velocity/acceleration limits, separating collision normals and penetration correction.
    9 | - Orange is Player 1; blue is Player 2/AI. Keep HUD outside play areas, retain black outlines, local fonts, rounded geometry and brief feedback. Do not reintroduce opacity-zero menu remounts.
   10 | - Duel results and arcade scores are separate. Core coordinates scoring and tournament attempt tokens; only a valid current attempt may score. Validate restored data. Preserve the legacy Pong ID `ping-pong`.
   11 | - Heavy AI runs in cancellable workers with time/node bounds. AI obeys human physics. Only Classic Tic-Tac-Toe claims optimal play; other Impossible modes are bounded practical searches.
   12 | - Run relevant unit checks, `npm run build`, browser regressions and `npm run test:bundle`. Run `test:modules` for discovery changes. Do not equate headless desktop Chrome with Android device validation.
   13 | - Android assets are packaged; web modules cache on first use, with an explicit offline download in Settings. No secrets, SDK paths, build outputs or credentials in source control. Never publish/deploy without the user's request.
~~~

## README.md
SHA-256: c96da9ece96fbf341625a1ed8a9b7ab0b6e2ee1d7a8785325010fad0cf51ccc1
~~~text
    1 | # Pocket Rivals
    2 | 
    3 | An original offline game collection for one phone: 15 local/AI rivalry games, two solo arcade games, Ultimate Golf’s own three modes, and persistent tournaments. TypeScript · Phaser 3 · Vite · Capacitor 8. The existing cream/pastel visual identity, local typography, bold outlines and illustrated cards are preserved.
    4 | 
    5 | ## Run
    6 | 
    7 | Requires Node 22.21.1+ and npm.
    8 | 
    9 | ```sh
   10 | npm ci
   11 | npm run dev             # http://127.0.0.1:5173/
   12 | npm run build           # Strict TypeScript + production dist/
   13 | npm run preview         # Production preview on port 4173
   14 | npm test                # Pure rules, physics, AI and persistence
   15 | npm run test:browser    # Installed Chrome, Pixel 7 emulation and CDP multi-touch
   16 | npm run test:modules    # Folder-only automatic discovery proof
   17 | npm run test:bundle     # Initial-payload budget and lazy-module verification
   18 | node scripts/measure-expansion.mjs # Running dev server required; desktop Chrome sample
   19 | ```
   20 | 
   21 | Build before running browser or bundle tests. Browser tests use installed Google Chrome; alternatively install Playwright Chromium and remove the channel override in `playwright.config.ts`. Vercel configuration is included; nothing has been deployed.
   22 | 
   23 | ## Play
   24 | 
   25 | | Collection      | Games                                                                   |
   26 | | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   27 | | 2 Player Games | Pong, Air Hockey, Tic-Tac-Toe (Classic/Ultimate), Connect Four, Dots and Boxes, Hammer Hit, Light Fingers, Fruit Duel, Math Quiz, Lumberjack, Water Guess, Perfect Timer, Gravity Runner, Happy Birds, Spike Attacks |
   28 | | 1 Player Arcade | Ultimate Golf, Classic Snake, Star Patrol                               |
   29 | | Tournament      | Any eligible rivalry game/variant; random or selected pool; local or AI |
   30 | 
   31 | Every rivalry game offers Medium, Hard and Impossible AI. Classic Impossible cannot be beaten with legal play; Ultimate and Connect Four use strong bounded searches, **not a mathematical optimality guarantee**. Blue is AI in single-player games. For most local games, orange plays below and blue above. Water Guess and Hammer Hit rotate the field for local Blue turns; playfield color identifies the active player.
   32 | 
   33 | - Pong/Hockey: first to five, or lead at two minutes. Regulation 0–0 draws; other ties get a 60-second sudden-death period, then draw. Hockey also awards a point against 15 seconds of continuous possession on one half.
   34 | - Ultimate: legal boards are highlighted; optional focus enlarges the required board. The interactive tutorial is in setup.
   35 | - Connect Four: tap a column.
   36 | - Ultimate Golf: four source-faithful courses with Casual, AI challenge, and local hot-seat competition. The uniformly scaled camera adapts to portrait and landscape. Pull back anywhere on the course and release; Focus enlarges the view, ? explains the course, R retries. Easy/Normal/Hard preserve the original obstacle speeds and stroke limits. [Port details](docs/ULTIMATE_GOLF.md).
   37 | - Snake: direction pad, swipe, arrows or WASD. Star Patrol: drag the lower field to move/fire, or arrows/A–D plus Space.
   38 | - Escape/back opens pause. Backgrounding pauses automatically. Settings retain sound-effects volume; no music track is included.
   39 | 
   40 | Completed duel scores, tournament progress, supported board/physics match checkpoints and arcade high scores are stored locally. New real-time duel attempts restart after application closure; pause/resume keeps the active attempt in memory. Golf keeps per-course best scores; active Arcade runs restart after closure. No accounts, ads, analytics, backend or external AI.
   41 | 
   42 | Android packages the full collection offline. The production web version caches the shell and games as played; use **Settings → Save all games offline** while connected to make every game and AI worker available without a network. Browser site-data eviction can remove that cache.
   43 | 
   44 | See [AI refinement](docs/AI_REFINEMENT.md), [formal review](docs/ANTIGRAVITY_REVIEW.md), and [seven-game expansion](docs/EXPANSION_COMPLETION.md) for implementation and test details.
   45 | 
   46 | ## Development
   47 | 
   48 | Open `/?diagnostics` in development for FPS/frame time, initialization timings, scenes, texture count, memory where supported, AI search time and loaded modules. The diagnostic UI and read-only test snapshots are disabled in production.
   49 | 
   50 | Start with [architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md), [adding games](docs/ADDING_GAMES.md), the root AGENTS.md and the target game's AGENTS.md. Each game owns its rules, physics, AI and assets. Only metadata is eager; implementations and workers are split into lazy chunks. The stable Pong ID remains `ping-pong`.
   51 | 
   52 | ## Android
   53 | 
   54 | ```sh
   55 | npm run android:sync    # Build and package all web assets
   56 | npm run android:open    # Open Android Studio
   57 | npm run android:debug   # Sync + assembleDebug
   58 | npm run android:release # Sync + signed bundleRelease
   59 | ```
   60 | 
   61 | Debug output: `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`. Release output: `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab`. This workstation lacks a usable Java runtime and Android SDK; no APK/AAB or physical-device testing is claimed. Android is configured with min SDK 24, compile/target SDK 36, portrait mode and no app permissions. See [build/signing instructions](docs/ANDROID_RELEASE.md).
   62 | 
   63 | [QA and known limits](docs/QA.md) · [Privacy/data handling](docs/PRIVACY.md) · [Third-party licenses](docs/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Branding and illustrations are original; fonts are bundled under their open licenses. Publisher identity/name/package availability and release signing remain the publisher's responsibility.
   64 | 
   65 | Flappy Jump, Car Duel, Archery Duel and Chicken Jump are preserved in [src/future-games](src/future-games/README.md) for later development. They are excluded from menus, tournaments and production bundles.
~~~

SHA-256: b187b4c52e749f5760afdd6fadc31b2a98ad35fb249bf0dff03b72650f320409
~~~text
    1 | #!/bin/sh
    2 | 
    3 | #
    4 | # Copyright © 2015-2021 the original authors.
    5 | #
    6 | # Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0 (the "License");
    7 | # you may not use this file except in compliance with the License.
    8 | # You may obtain a copy of the License at
    9 | #
   10 | #      https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0
   11 | #
   12 | # Unless required by applicable law or agreed to in writing, software
   13 | # distributed under the License is distributed on an "AS IS" BASIS,
   14 | # WITHOUT WARRANTIES OR CONDITIONS OF ANY KIND, either express or implied.
   15 | # See the License for the specific language governing permissions and
   16 | # limitations under the License.
   17 | #
   18 | # SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
   19 | #
   20 | 
   21 | ##############################################################################
   22 | #
   23 | #   Gradle start up script for POSIX generated by Gradle.
   24 | #
   25 | #   Important for running:
   26 | #
   27 | #   (1) You need a POSIX-compliant shell to run this script. If your /bin/sh is
   28 | #       noncompliant, but you have some other compliant shell such as ksh or
   29 | #       bash, then to run this script, type that shell name before the whole
   30 | #       command line, like:
   31 | #
   32 | #           ksh Gradle
   33 | #
   34 | #       Busybox and similar reduced shells will NOT work, because this script
   35 | #       requires all of these POSIX shell features:
   36 | #         * functions;
   37 | #         * expansions «$var», «${var}», «${var:-default}», «${var+SET}»,
   38 | #           «${var#prefix}», «${var%suffix}», and «$( cmd )»;
   39 | #         * compound commands having a testable exit status, especially «case»;
   40 | #         * various built-in commands including «command», «set», and «ulimit».
   41 | #
   42 | #   Important for patching:
   43 | #
   44 | #   (2) This script targets any POSIX shell, so it avoids extensions provided
   45 | #       by Bash, Ksh, etc; in particular arrays are avoided.
   46 | #
   47 | #       The "traditional" practice of packing multiple parameters into a
   48 | #       space-separated string is a well documented source of bugs and security
   49 | #       problems, so this is (mostly) avoided, by progressively accumulating
   50 | #       options in "$@", and eventually passing that to Java.
   51 | #
   52 | #       Where the inherited environment variables (DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS, JAVA_OPTS,
   53 | #       and GRADLE_OPTS) rely on word-splitting, this is performed explicitly;
   54 | #       see the in-line comments for details.
   55 | #
   56 | #       There are tweaks for specific operating systems such as AIX, CygWin,
   57 | #       Darwin, MinGW, and NonStop.
   58 | #
   59 | #   (3) This script is generated from the Groovy template
   60 | #       https://github.com/gradle/gradle/blob/HEAD/platforms/jvm/plugins-application/src/main/resources/org/gradle/api/internal/plugins/unixStartScript.txt
   61 | #       within the Gradle project.
   62 | #
   63 | #       You can find Gradle at https://github.com/gradle/gradle/.
   64 | #
   65 | ##############################################################################
   66 | 
   67 | # Attempt to set APP_HOME
   68 | 
   69 | # Resolve links: $0 may be a link
   70 | app_path=$0
   71 | 
   72 | # Need this for daisy-chained symlinks.
   73 | while
   74 |     APP_HOME=${app_path%"${app_path##*/}"}  # leaves a trailing /; empty if no leading path
   75 |     [ -h "$app_path" ]
   76 | do
   77 |     ls=$( ls -ld "$app_path" )
   78 |     link=${ls#*' -> '}
   79 |     case $link in             #(
   80 |       /*)   app_path=$link ;; #(
   81 |       *)    app_path=$APP_HOME$link ;;
   82 |     esac
   83 | done
   84 | 
   85 | # This is normally unused
   86 | # shellcheck disable=SC2034
   87 | APP_BASE_NAME=${0##*/}
   88 | # Discard cd standard output in case $CDPATH is set (https://github.com/gradle/gradle/issues/25036)
   89 | APP_HOME=$( cd -P "${APP_HOME:-./}" > /dev/null && printf '%s\n' "$PWD" ) || exit
   90 | 
   91 | # Use the maximum available, or set MAX_FD != -1 to use that value.
   92 | MAX_FD=maximum
   93 | 
   94 | warn () {
   95 |     echo "$*"
   96 | } >&2
   97 | 
   98 | die () {
   99 |     echo
  100 |     echo "$*"
  101 |     echo
  102 |     exit 1
  103 | } >&2
  104 | 
  105 | # OS specific support (must be 'true' or 'false').
  106 | cygwin=false
  107 | msys=false
  108 | darwin=false
  109 | nonstop=false
  110 | case "$( uname )" in                #(
  111 |   CYGWIN* )         cygwin=true  ;; #(
  112 |   Darwin* )         darwin=true  ;; #(
  113 |   MSYS* | MINGW* )  msys=true    ;; #(
  114 |   NONSTOP* )        nonstop=true ;;
  115 | esac
  116 | 
  117 | CLASSPATH="\\\"\\\""
  118 | 
  119 | 
  120 | # Determine the Java command to use to start the JVM.
  121 | if [ -n "$JAVA_HOME" ] ; then
  122 |     if [ -x "$JAVA_HOME/jre/sh/java" ] ; then
  123 |         # IBM's JDK on AIX uses strange locations for the executables
  124 |         JAVACMD=$JAVA_HOME/jre/sh/java
  125 |     else
  126 |         JAVACMD=$JAVA_HOME/bin/java
  127 |     fi
  128 |     if [ ! -x "$JAVACMD" ] ; then
  129 |         die "ERROR: JAVA_HOME is set to an invalid directory: $JAVA_HOME
  130 | 
  131 | Please set the JAVA_HOME variable in your environment to match the
  132 | location of your Java installation."
  133 |     fi
  134 | else
  135 |     JAVACMD=java
  136 |     if ! command -v java >/dev/null 2>&1
  137 |     then
  138 |         die "ERROR: JAVA_HOME is not set and no 'java' command could be found in your PATH.
  139 | 
  140 | Please set the JAVA_HOME variable in your environment to match the
  141 | location of your Java installation."
  142 |     fi
  143 | fi
  144 | 
  145 | # Increase the maximum file descriptors if we can.
  146 | if ! "$cygwin" && ! "$darwin" && ! "$nonstop" ; then
  147 |     case $MAX_FD in #(
  148 |       max*)
  149 |         # In POSIX sh, ulimit -H is undefined. That's why the result is checked to see if it worked.
  150 |         # shellcheck disable=SC2039,SC3045
  151 |         MAX_FD=$( ulimit -H -n ) ||
  152 |             warn "Could not query maximum file descriptor limit"
  153 |     esac
  154 |     case $MAX_FD in  #(
  155 |       '' | soft) :;; #(
  156 |       *)
  157 |         # In POSIX sh, ulimit -n is undefined. That's why the result is checked to see if it worked.
  158 |         # shellcheck disable=SC2039,SC3045
  159 |         ulimit -n "$MAX_FD" ||
  160 |             warn "Could not set maximum file descriptor limit to $MAX_FD"
  161 |     esac
  162 | fi
  163 | 
  164 | # Collect all arguments for the java command, stacking in reverse order:
  165 | #   * args from the command line
  166 | #   * the main class name
  167 | #   * -classpath
  168 | #   * -D...appname settings
  169 | #   * --module-path (only if needed)
  170 | #   * DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS, JAVA_OPTS, and GRADLE_OPTS environment variables.
  171 | 
  172 | # For Cygwin or MSYS, switch paths to Windows format before running java
  173 | if "$cygwin" || "$msys" ; then
  174 |     APP_HOME=$( cygpath --path --mixed "$APP_HOME" )
  175 |     CLASSPATH=$( cygpath --path --mixed "$CLASSPATH" )
  176 | 
  177 |     JAVACMD=$( cygpath --unix "$JAVACMD" )
  178 | 
  179 |     # Now convert the arguments - kludge to limit ourselves to /bin/sh
  180 |     for arg do
  181 |         if
  182 |             case $arg in                                #(
  183 |               -*)   false ;;                            # don't mess with options #(
  184 |               /?*)  t=${arg#/} t=/${t%%/*}              # looks like a POSIX filepath
  185 |                     [ -e "$t" ] ;;                      #(
  186 |               *)    false ;;
  187 |             esac
  188 |         then
  189 |             arg=$( cygpath --path --ignore --mixed "$arg" )
  190 |         fi
  191 |         # Roll the args list around exactly as many times as the number of
  192 |         # args, so each arg winds up back in the position where it started, but
  193 |         # possibly modified.
  194 |         #
  195 |         # NB: a `for` loop captures its iteration list before it begins, so
  196 |         # changing the positional parameters here affects neither the number of
  197 |         # iterations, nor the values presented in `arg`.
  198 |         shift                   # remove old arg
  199 |         set -- "$@" "$arg"      # push replacement arg
  200 |     done
  201 | fi
  202 | 
  203 | 
  204 | # Add default JVM options here. You can also use JAVA_OPTS and GRADLE_OPTS to pass JVM options to this script.
  205 | DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS='"-Xmx64m" "-Xms64m"'
  206 | 
  207 | # Collect all arguments for the java command:
  208 | #   * DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS, JAVA_OPTS, and optsEnvironmentVar are not allowed to contain shell fragments,
  209 | #     and any embedded shellness will be escaped.
  210 | #   * For example: A user cannot expect ${Hostname} to be expanded, as it is an environment variable and will be
  211 | #     treated as '${Hostname}' itself on the command line.
  212 | 
  213 | set -- \
  214 |         "-Dorg.gradle.appname=$APP_BASE_NAME" \
  215 |         -classpath "$CLASSPATH" \
  216 |         -jar "$APP_HOME/gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.jar" \
  217 |         "$@"
  218 | 
  219 | # Stop when "xargs" is not available.
  220 | if ! command -v xargs >/dev/null 2>&1
  221 | then
  222 |     die "xargs is not available"
  223 | fi
  224 | 
  225 | # Use "xargs" to parse quoted args.
  226 | #
  227 | # With -n1 it outputs one arg per line, with the quotes and backslashes removed.
  228 | #
  229 | # In Bash we could simply go:
  230 | #
  231 | #   readarray ARGS < <( xargs -n1 <<<"$var" ) &&
  232 | #   set -- "${ARGS[@]}" "$@"
  233 | #
  234 | # but POSIX shell has neither arrays nor command substitution, so instead we
  235 | # post-process each arg (as a line of input to sed) to backslash-escape any
  236 | # character that might be a shell metacharacter, then use eval to reverse
  237 | # that process (while maintaining the separation between arguments), and wrap
  238 | # the whole thing up as a single "set" statement.
  239 | #
  240 | # This will of course break if any of these variables contains a newline or
  241 | # an unmatched quote.
  242 | #
  243 | 
  244 | eval "set -- $(
  245 |         printf '%s\n' "$DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS $JAVA_OPTS $GRADLE_OPTS" |
  246 |         xargs -n1 |
  247 |         sed ' s~[^-[:alnum:]+,./:=@_]~\\&~g; ' |
  248 |         tr '\n' ' '
  249 |     )" '"$@"'
  250 | 
  251 | exec "$JAVACMD" "$@"
~~~

   46 | if %ERRORLEVEL% equ 0 goto execute

   49 | echo ERROR: JAVA_HOME is not set and no 'java' command could be found in your PATH. 1>&2
   50 | echo. 1>&2
   51 | echo Please set the JAVA_HOME variable in your environment to match the 1>&2
   52 | echo location of your Java installation. 1>&2
   53 | 
   54 | goto fail
   55 | 
   56 | :findJavaFromJavaHome
   57 | set JAVA_HOME=%JAVA_HOME:"=%
   58 | set JAVA_EXE=%JAVA_HOME%/bin/java.exe
   59 | 
   60 | if exist "%JAVA_EXE%" goto execute

   64 | echo. 1>&2
   65 | echo Please set the JAVA_HOME variable in your environment to match the 1>&2
   66 | echo location of your Java installation. 1>&2
   67 | 
   68 | goto fail

   74 | 
   75 |

   77 | "%JAVA_EXE%" %DEFAULT_JVM_OPTS% %JAVA_OPTS% %GRADLE_OPTS% "-Dorg.gradle.appname=%APP_BASE_NAME%" -classpath "%CLASSPATH%" -jar "%APP_HOME%\gradle\wrapper\gradle-wrapper.jar" %*
   78 | 
   79 | :end

   81 | if %ERRORLEVEL% equ 0 goto mainEnd

   85 | rem the _cmd.exe /c_ return code!
   86 | set EXIT_CODE=%ERRORLEVEL%
   87 | if %EXIT_CODE% equ 0 set EXIT_CODE=1
   88 | if not ""=="%GRADLE_EXIT_CONSOLE%" exit %EXIT_CODE%
   89 | exit /b %EXIT_CODE%

   91 | :mainEnd
   92 | if "%OS%"=="Windows_NT" endlocal
   93 | 
   94 | :omega

## docs/ADDING_GAMES.md
SHA-256: 0886c969abdb1ef3668b4eea73c9cf431f9f3630959f086e66eb3a330191e07e
~~~text
    1 | # Add a game without editing core
    2 | 
    3 | 1. Create `src/games/<folder>/` for a duel, or `src/arcade/<folder>/` for a solo arcade game.
    4 | 2. Add `config.ts`, `index.ts`, your implementation, and a small original SVG preview.
    5 | 3. Implement `MiniGame` from `src/shared/contracts/GameModule.ts`.
    6 | 4. Run tests and rebuild. Metadata discovery, the menu, lazy loader and eligible tournaments update automatically.
    7 | 
    8 | No edits to registry, router, score manager, menu or another game are needed. The folder name need not equal the stable game ID. Installation is **build time**, not runtime plugin downloading.
    9 | 
   10 | ## Metadata
   11 | 
   12 | ```ts
   13 | import type { GameMetadata } from "../../shared/contracts/GameModule";
   14 | import preview from "./assets/preview.svg?raw";
   15 | export default {
   16 |   id: "tap-duel",
   17 |   name: "Tap Duel",
   18 |   description: "A little race for your thumbs.",
   19 |   instructions: "Tap your own half. First to ten wins.",
   20 |   color: "#f3bdab",
   21 |   accent: "#fffdf5",
   22 |   preview,
   23 |   order: 20,
   24 |   tag: "QUICK FINGERS",
   25 |   category: "duel",
   26 |   tournament: true,
   27 |   supportedModes: ["local-two-player"],
   28 | } satisfies GameMetadata;
   29 | ```
   30 | 
   31 | Declare `single-player` only if AI is implemented for duels. Unsupported AI is disabled in setup and excluded from AI tournament pools. Optional `variants` contain IDs, display names, descriptions, `ai: false` overrides and `hasTutorial`. Your factory receives `MatchOptions` and may lazily import the selected variant. An optional named `tutorial(variant, ui)` export owns that game's tutorial.
   32 | 
   33 | ## Working example
   34 | 
   35 | `examples/tap-duel/` is a complete, playable implementation, not part of the shipped collection. Copy that folder unchanged into `src/games/tap-duel/`, then run `npm run build`. It demonstrates input, independent state, score reporting and disposal. `npm run test:modules` performs this copy in a temporary checkout and verifies discovery/build without changing the real collection.
   36 | 
   37 | Its factory is simply:
   38 | 
   39 | ```ts
   40 | export default () => new TapDuel();
   41 | ```
   42 | 
   43 | The class implements:
   44 | 
   45 | ```ts
   46 | initialize(ctx: GameContext): void; // Create objects and bind input here.
   47 | update(elapsedSeconds: number): void;
   48 | pause(): void;   // Clear transient controls; cancel AI work.
   49 | resume(): void;
   50 | dispose(): void; // Destroy objects, remove owned assets, terminate workers.
   51 | snapshot?(): unknown; // Optional development observability, not mutable controls.
   52 | ```
   53 | 
   54 | Use `ctx.setScore(one, two)`, `ctx.setHint(text)`, optional `ctx.setClock(text, urgent)`, and exactly one `ctx.finish({ winner: 1 | 2 | 'draw', scores: [one, two] })`. Winner is explicit; low-score games such as golf work without special tournament logic. Never update global scores yourself.
   55 | 
   56 | For Arcade, declare `category: 'arcade'`, `tournament: false`, `supportedModes: ['single-player']`. Use `ctx.bestScore`, `ctx.setArcadeHUD(score, detail)` and `ctx.finishArcade(score, detail)` instead of duel results. Core persists the high score independently.
   57 | 
   58 | ## Isolation and performance checklist
   59 | 
   60 | - Keep rules, physics, AI, course data and save validation in the module. No cross-game imports.
   61 | - Do not import implementation code from `config.ts`; it is eagerly evaluated. Use only lightweight SVG previews there.
   62 | - Constructors/factories must have no side effects. Create listeners, workers and objects only in `initialize` or a cancellable decision.
   63 | - Use the supplied scene; never create another Phaser.Game or rendering loop. Coordinates are logical 420×760; shared HUD lies outside the playfield.
   64 | - `ctx.input.tap`, `dragHalves`, `drag`, `press` and `keys` are host-cleaned and pause-aware. Any additional subscription must have its own cleanup.
   65 | - Use fixed-step simulation for physics. Use foreground elapsed time for real clocks. Never tick time by frame count.
   66 | - Use `WorkerTask` for costly search. Workers should return within a bounded budget, report `milliseconds`, and terminate on pause/dispose. Call `ctx.reportAI` for diagnostics.
   67 | - Call `ctx.saveState` only with compact serializable data. Validate `ctx.restoredState`; reject malformed histories rather than trusting stored cells. Checkpoint after discrete moves or at a modest frequency.
   68 | - Namespace dynamic textures; remove them on disposal. Do not allocate graphics/text or unbounded particles each frame.
   69 | - Test rules, illegal input, results, pause, stale worker cancellation, saves, repeated navigation, mobile layout and offline worker loading. Add a concise module AGENTS.md.
   70 | 
   71 | ## Commands
   72 | 
   73 | ```sh
   74 | npm run dev
   75 | npm test
   76 | npm run build
   77 | npm run test:browser
   78 | npm run test:modules
   79 | npm run test:bundle
   80 | npm run android:sync
   81 | npm run android:debug
   82 | npm run android:release # Requires local signing environment variables
   83 | ```
   84 | 
   85 | `test:bundle` discovers the expected folders automatically, verifies their lazy chunks and enforces an application-shell size budget. Review the report when adding games; no module-count expectation or application core change is needed. Android signing/build prerequisites are in `docs/ANDROID_RELEASE.md`.
   86 | 
   87 | ## Additional reference modules
   88 | 
   89 | - `src/future-games/chicken-jump`: small fixed-step timing game, seeded AI and geometric landings.
   90 | - `src/future-games/archery-duel`: debounced multi-step input and delayed, idempotent impact scoring.
   91 | - `spike-attacks`: swept collisions, bounded per-wave path planning and independent arenas.
   92 | - `src/future-games/car-duel`: deferred module with custom rigid-body approximation and explicitly disposed multi-pointer controls.
   93 | 
   94 | Declare timeout/tie rules in metadata. Test terminal guards, identical local conditions, input cancellation, pause/resume and actual scoring paths. Use a unique new test filename; preserve existing regression tests. Do not claim checkpoint support unless a module validates and restores its own state.
~~~

## docs/AI_REFINEMENT.md
SHA-256: 3ec53644ced4236cb7847c411d3ca722daba4eda4b9213c1656cd5720f3bc78e
~~~text
    1 | # AI refinement
    2 | 
    3 | Scope: Pong, Air Hockey, Classic and Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe, Connect Four, Dots and Boxes, Hammer Hit, Light Fingers, Fruit Duel, Lumberjack, and the active Ultimate Golf port. Math Quiz is owned by concurrent development and was not edited. Water Guess and Perfect Timer appeared during concurrent development and already use the seeded utility; their implementations were inspected read-only and left to their owner. Concurrent Pong keyboard-control edits were also preserved. The proposed racing and other survival modules are not present; Snake and Star Patrol have no opponent AI.
    4 | 
    5 | ## Match identity and replay
    6 | 
    7 | `shared/ai/MatchRandom.ts` is a small, lazy utility, not a game manager. Each opponent receives a fresh cryptographic seed and a persistent identity. The 24 profile slots combine four game-specific roles, three tempo/position settings and two side preferences. These are parameters of each game's decisions, not 24 copied algorithms. Simple reflex games and solved positions naturally have less tactical variety.
    8 | 
    9 | Development URL: `/?aiSeed=314159&aiReplay&diagnostics`.
   10 | 
   11 | - `aiSeed` pins the seed; normal matches/rematches generate a new seed.
   12 | - `aiReplay` substitutes bounded node/candidate limits for wall-clock search cutoffs. Given the same position and seed, worker decisions replay. Normal production searches retain time limits.
   13 | - Physics replay also requires the same timestep and human input stream. This is not an input recorder. Worker watchdog cancellation can still interrupt a debug search on slow devices.
   14 | - `window.__POCKET__.scene.game.ai` contains identity and, where applicable, the current target/reaction. Golf exposes this under `competition.ai`.
   15 | - Existing board and physics checkpoints retain the identity seed. A board move derives its randomness from the seed and position. A physics checkpoint retains the personality, not every transient movement-controller/RNG accumulator.
   16 | - Goal/course resets preserve identity. Fresh matches create a new one. Pausing freezes simulation and terminates search workers; stale generations cannot play moves after exit.
   17 | 
   18 | ## Changes and causes
   19 | 
   20 | | Game           | Original repetition                                                                 | Current decisions                                                                                                                                                                                  |
   21 | | -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
   22 | | Classic TTT    | First move in a fixed ordering won every minimax tie                                | Weighted seeded choice among exactly equal scores; center, corner, edge and flank preferences. Hard resolves opening equivalence with full search. Impossible always uses full minimax.            |
   23 | | Ultimate TTT   | Fixed ordering, fixed positional weights; root bounds unsuitable for tie comparison | Stable seeded ordering, modest local/global positional preferences, exact root comparisons, existing iterative deepening and transposition bounds.                                                 |
   24 | | Connect Four   | Center-first tie selection and one evaluator                                        | Aggressive, defensive, balanced and flank emphasis; positional weights and equal-score selection vary. Immediate wins retain priority; terminal scores dominate preferences.                       |
   25 | | Dots and Boxes | Same greedy opening, fixed chain evaluation; some bounds cached as exact            | Perimeter, center, horizontal and flank preferences; chain valuation; correct upper/lower/exact cache entries and full-window root comparisons.                                                    |
   26 | | Pong           | Same interception and outgoing central tracking                                     | Angle attacker, defender, counter and flank preferences. Shot angle locks per incoming flight and uses the opponent's observed paddle; difficult interceptions abandon risky offsets.              |
   27 | | Air Hockey     | One home position and approach pattern                                              | Pressure, guard, counter and positional home/approach parameters; observed opponent positioning guides shots. Approach-side commitment avoids target flipping.                                     |
   28 | | Light Fingers  | Narrow uniform delay                                                                | Match cadence plus per-signal bounded bell-shaped reaction time; pressure-sensitive Hard/Medium behavior, visible-signal-only input and a 120 ms minimum.                                          |
   29 | | Fruit Duel     | Narrow uniform delay and fixed recognition-error rate                               | Cadence and cautious/opportunistic recognition profiles; per-reveal delay/error decisions. Impossible has no deliberate recognition errors.                                                        |
   30 | | Hammer Hit     | One threshold for all three strikes                                                 | Per-attempt precision tolerance and cadence parameters; Impossible aims for the best visible timing. Identical high scores are legitimate in this simple timing game.                              |
   31 | | Lumberjack     | Always chose left when safe; artificial Impossible mistake                          | Side preference, low-switching and visible-segment lookahead, varied legal chop cadence. Impossible never intentionally chooses a branch.                                                          |
   32 | | Ultimate Golf  | Fixed candidate order/delay; a periodic angle error applied after simulation        | Persistent planning preferences for waiting/bounce risk, seeded angle ordering and power refinement, variable shot preparation. Every executed trajectory was simulated by the real course engine. |
   33 | 
   34 | Difficulty remains game-specific. Medium uses shallower searches, slower reactions and occasional legal recognition/position errors. Hard increases tactical search and accuracy. Impossible removes deliberate reflex errors, uses maximum search budgets and precise legal motion. Only Classic TTT claims optimal play. Repeated forced wins, draws or identical strong moves are not treated as defects.
   35 | 
   36 | ## Performance and boundaries
   37 | 
   38 | No dependencies were added. No rule engine, scoring, tournament, registry, rendering or shared motion-controller behavior was changed. AI implementations remain in their game folders. Search workers keep cancellation and the existing two-second watchdog. Normal worker budgets are 25/100/300 ms for Connect Four, 25/100/280 ms for Ultimate, 12/70/180 ms for Dots, and 65/140/240 ms for Golf (Medium/Hard/Impossible). Dots Medium is greedy. Golf evaluates complete trajectories between budget checks, so a single trial may slightly exceed its budget.
   39 | 
   40 | Pong and Hockey keep acceleration limits, interpolated targets, legal field constraints and deadbands. Randomness is sampled at tactical/reaction boundaries, never independently each render frame. No score changes, teleports or physics exemptions were added.
   41 | 
   42 | ## Verification
   43 | 
   44 | Run:
   45 | 
   46 | ```sh
   47 | AI_AUDIT=1 npx vitest run tests/unit/ai-refinement.test.ts
   48 | npx vitest run --exclude '**/math-quiz.test.ts'
   49 | npx vitest run --config tests/fixtures/golf-audit.config.ts
   50 | npx playwright test tests/browser/ai-refinement.spec.ts tests/browser/phase2.spec.ts tests/browser/phase3.spec.ts
   51 | npm run build
   52 | npm run test:bundle
   53 | npm run test:modules
   54 | ```
   55 | 
   56 | `docs/ai-audit.json` contains seed/profile/difficulty, decisions, scores, simulation duration and measured host CPU timings. It covers 100 matches per difficulty for Classic and each of four reflex/survival games, 100 Medium Dots matches, strategy scenarios and Golf replay checks. Physics uses 100 scenarios per difficulty at 30/60/120 Hz rather than claiming full-match coverage. Exhaustive legal human continuations test Classic Impossible from both player positions across all 24 profile slots. Tests also cover difficulty separation, legal movement, terminal-state guards and worker replay.
   57 | 
   58 | A live development server can reload during concurrent edits. Final browser regressions use an unchanged temporary snapshot of the same source to avoid HMR interference. This is headless desktop Chrome with touch emulation, not a physical Android or memory-soak certification. Android device feel, long-session heap behavior and broader Golf seed/course combinations still need device playtesting.
   59 | 
   60 | ## Recorded results (initial AI pass)
   61 | 
   62 | - 202 non-Math unit tests passed; the concurrent Math module's 7 tests subsequently passed in a separate read-only run. Earlier Math failures were left to its owner.
   63 | - 1,600 complete scripted lightweight matches: 100 per difficulty in Classic, Light Fingers, Fruit Duel, Hammer Hit and Lumberjack, plus 100 Medium Dots matches. These benchmark opponents are scripted, not estimates of human win rates.
   64 | - 300 paired Pong/Hockey scenarios, at 30/60/120 Hz, verified movement bounds and finite physics. Existing high-speed collision and 60,000-step stability regressions also pass.
   65 | - All nine Classic opening cells appeared across seeds at every difficulty. Classic Impossible remained unbeaten against all legal human continuations for representatives of all 24 personalities, playing either side.
   66 | - Light Fingers' mean sampled opening reactions were 524.6/287.1/143.7 ms; Hammer's mean strike scores were 76.57/94.88/99.67 for Medium/Hard/Impossible. The narrow Impossible score range is expected, not artificially widened.
   67 | - All four original Golf route audits completed under the revised planner. Eight seeded Hard shot scenarios confirmed comparable-shot diversity; seeded planner replay checks pass. This does not certify every seed on every course.
   68 | - Production Vite build, automatic-module discovery check and bundle check pass. The current shell is 21,183 bytes gzip; total initial JavaScript is 355,905 bytes gzip, mostly Phaser. AI modules and `MatchRandom` are absent from the initial static import graph. Concurrently added game metadata is included in these totals.
   69 | - Audit records label shared simulation CPU as `cpuBatch`; strategy/Golf records use measured search CPU. Turn-based `duration` is a synthetic thinking-time estimate; reflex/survival durations are measured simulation time. Physics records are two-second scenarios, not full matches.
   70 | - 25 distinct browser scenarios passed across the stable-snapshot runs, including tournaments, lazy loading, real touch/mouse play, Golf AI, saved identities and pause/exit worker cleanup. Two real-time input checks (Fruit and Snake) failed under a heavily loaded run and passed unchanged on isolated rerun; they remain timing-sensitive tests. The final six AI/Golf browser checks passed together in 1.1 minutes.
   71 | 
   72 | ## Follow-up integration
   73 | 
   74 | The subsequent review and seven-game expansion are recorded in EXPANSION_COMPLETION.md and ANTIGRAVITY_REVIEW.md. Hammer now uses alternating full-field turns with 1.2–1.5 seconds of AI preparation before legal gauge timing. Classic/Ultimate/Connect Four have a visible minimum thinking delay; this changes presentation, not search strength. The later Golf route selector now avalanche-mixes seed/role values to prevent low-bit aliasing. Newer Golf stroke-first competition rules were preserved during integration.
~~~

## docs/ANDROID_RELEASE.md
SHA-256: cab8d633460dfc72916ffc7cd81aadba3922adedddd3963a8a727f6a951f3b3d
~~~text
    1 | # Android build and Google Play preparation
    2 | 
    3 | Status as of **2026-10-13**: Capacitor Android project generated and configured. Java/Android SDK are unavailable on this workstation; native compilation, emulator execution and device testing remain outstanding. No publication has been attempted.
    4 | 
    5 | ## Toolchain
    6 | 
    7 | Install Android Studio **Otter 2025.2.1 or newer**, its bundled JDK 21, Android SDK Platform 36, Android SDK Build-Tools, command-line tools, and platform tools. Accept Android SDK licenses through Android Studio. Use Node 22.21.1+ and `npm ci`.
    8 | 
    9 | On macOS, if the shell cannot find Android Studio's Java runtime:
   10 | 
   11 | ```sh
   12 | export JAVA_HOME="/Applications/Android Studio.app/Contents/jbr/Contents/Home"
   13 | export ANDROID_HOME="$HOME/Library/Android/sdk"
   14 | export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$PATH"
   15 | ```
   16 | 
   17 | Android Studio can write `android/local.properties` with your SDK path; this file is ignored and must not be committed. Do not change the repository's Gradle wrapper to an unrelated globally installed Gradle.
   18 | 
   19 | ## Debug APK
   20 | 
   21 | ```sh
   22 | npm ci
   23 | npm test
   24 | npm run build
   25 | npm run test:browser
   26 | npm run android:debug
   27 | ```
   28 | 
   29 | Install `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk` on a device, or use:
   30 | 
   31 | ```sh
   32 | adb install -r android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
   33 | ```
   34 | 
   35 | After adding/changing games, repeat `npm run android:debug`; it rebuilds the web app and synchronizes the bundled assets before compiling. Debug and release assets have no development-server URL configured.
   36 | 
   37 | ## Identity and versions
   38 | 
   39 | - Proposed application ID / Java namespace: `com.pocketrivals.games`.
   40 | - Display name: **Pocket Rivals**.
   41 | - Android minimum API: **24**; compile and target API: **36**.
   42 | - Default Android versionCode: **1**; versionName: **0.3.0**.
   43 | - Web package version: `package.json`.
   44 | 
   45 | Before the first Play upload, confirm ownership/availability of the identity and name. If changing the ID, update `capacitor.config.ts`, `android/app/build.gradle`, strings `package_name` and `custom_url_scheme`, and the Java package declaration/directory under `android/app/src/main/java`. This identity becomes permanent for an existing Play listing.
   46 | 
   47 | Override versions for each release through Gradle project properties:
   48 | 
   49 | ```sh
   50 | export ORG_GRADLE_PROJECT_appVersionCode=2
   51 | export ORG_GRADLE_PROJECT_appVersionName=0.1.1
   52 | npm run android:release
   53 | ```
   54 | 
   55 | Every Play upload needs a higher integer versionCode. Keep the displayed version in `package.json` and the settings UI in sync with versionName.
   56 | 
   57 | ## Signing without repository secrets
   58 | 
   59 | Use **Google Play App Signing**. Play protects the distribution signing key; sign uploaded AABs with your separate upload key. Create the upload key outside this repository (the command prompts for passwords):
   60 | 
   61 | ```sh
   62 | keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore /absolute/private/path/pocket-upload.jks \
   63 |   -alias pocket-upload -keyalg RSA -keysize 3072 -validity 10000
   64 | ```
   65 | 
   66 | Provide the following environment variables through your secret manager or an interactive shell. Never paste real values into documentation, chat, shell history, or source:
   67 | 
   68 | - `POCKET_KEYSTORE`: absolute path to the upload keystore.
   69 | - `POCKET_STORE_PASSWORD`: keystore password.
   70 | - `POCKET_KEY_ALIAS`: alias, e.g. `pocket-upload`.
   71 | - `POCKET_KEY_PASSWORD`: private-key password.
   72 | 
   73 | Then run `npm run android:release`. Release tasks fail with a clear message if any signing value is missing. They never silently use a debug key. Output: `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab`. Back up the upload key securely and use CI secret storage if you automate releases. Keystores and `.env` files are ignored.
   74 | 
   75 | ## Target SDK and native behavior
   76 | 
   77 | Google Play's current published requirement for new standard Android apps and updates is **Android 16 / API 36 or higher**. This project targets 36. Recheck the policy at submission; meeting target SDK alone is not full Play compliance.
   78 | 
   79 | Sources checked 2026-10-13:
   80 | 
   81 | - [Google Play target API requirements](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/11926878?hl=en-EN).
   82 | - [Capacitor 8 Android toolchain and API requirements](https://capacitorjs.com/docs/updating/8-0).
   83 | - [Google Play App Signing](https://developer.android.com/studio/publish/app-signing).
   84 | 
   85 | The manifest requests no app permissions, removes the template's internet permission and FileProvider, disables backup, and disallows cleartext traffic. No billing/ads/networking plugins are included. Capacitor serves packaged files through its local WebView bridge. Verify the final merged manifest after a native build to confirm library contributions. Test Android 16 edge-to-edge/safe-area behavior on hardware; the layout consumes Capacitor's CSS inset variables. Native phones request portrait; tablets/adaptive windows may ignore orientation restrictions, so the game also fits landscape containers.
   86 | 
   87 | The app pauses on `appStateChange`, browser visibility loss, and window blur. Android Back pauses gameplay; another Back resumes. Back from results returns to the menu. At the main menu it presents a close/stay dialog. No active game progresses while backgrounded.
   88 | 
   89 | ## Publisher release checklist
   90 | 
   91 | - [ ] Install toolchain; build debug APK; install on at least two physical Android devices.
   92 | - [ ] Test two real fingers from opposite ends: small/large phones, edge gestures, touch cancellation, and three simultaneous contacts.
   93 | - [ ] Play all seven games to completion; test goals near posts/rails, high-speed hits and repeated rematches.
   94 | - [ ] Measure frame times and touch responsiveness on a typical lower/mid-range Android device. The 60 FPS target is not a measured device guarantee yet.
   95 | - [ ] Test Home/lock/unlock, system Back, interruptions, audio focus, screen rotation, notches, gesture/button navigation and tablets.
   96 | - [ ] Test installation and full play in airplane mode. Verify scores after restart and after app update. Uninstall/clear-data intentionally removes scores.
   97 | - [ ] Check merged manifest, release dependency graph, Android lint, release logs and App Bundle contents. Check any transitive native libraries for 16 KB page-size support; none are intentionally added by the game.
   98 | - [ ] Confirm brand/package identity; retain font/dependency licenses and original artwork records.
   99 | - [ ] Set unique versionCode/versionName; sign the AAB with a securely stored upload key; enroll in Play App Signing.
  100 | - [ ] Use internal/closed testing, Play pre-launch reports, and any current testing prerequisites for the publisher's account.
  101 | - [ ] Prepare screenshots, 512 px store icon and 1024×500 feature graphic from the final product; do not reuse reference-game images.
  102 | - [ ] Complete content rating, target audience, Data safety, advertising declaration (none), and a public privacy-policy URL after adding the publisher's contact information.
  103 | - [ ] Obtain the publisher's explicit approval before any store submission or paid account creation.
~~~

## docs/ANTIGRAVITY_REVIEW.md
SHA-256: c5983ccfe258592b45f954b2214b0771a369172666a3d52c2246fab0760015ae
~~~text
    1 | # Formal review — Water Guess, Perfect Timer, Hammer Hit
    2 | 
    3 | Scope: preserve Antigravity's artwork and mechanics; inspect rules, AI, input, scoring, lifecycle and integration. Math Quiz source, question banks, rendering and AI were excluded from edits. Its tests ran read-only.
    4 | 
    5 | ## Confirmed findings and repairs
    6 | 
    7 | | Finding | Severity | Resolution |
    8 | |---|---|---|
    9 | | Perfect Timer included pause/background wall time in human stops and AI deadlines | High | Module-local foreground monotonic clock shared by both input paths; repeated pause/resume tested |
   10 | | AI stop and timeout could resolve the same round twice | High | Idempotent rule resolution plus controller phase guards |
   11 | | Both rules accepted nonfinite numeric submissions | Medium | Reject invalid values before updating state |
   12 | | Water Guess swallowed NumpadDecimal as a digit prefix | Medium | Restrict digit matching; browser decimal-key regression |
   13 | | Perfect Timer used identical preset order every match | Medium | Seeded selection without replacement |
   14 | | Both new AIs imposed artificial minimum error | Medium | Impossible Timer targets the visible exact duration; Water measures the visible tube to one logical pixel. Lower levels use seeded bias/variation |
   15 | | Hammer's inactive gauge advanced before its turn, allowing an immediate AI strike | Medium | Reset the active gauge on handoff, add 1.2–1.5s AI preparation, block input through strike animation |
   16 | | Old Hammer browser test assumed simultaneous play after controller changed to alternating turns | Test mismatch | Updated to validate six alternating strikes and arithmetic averages |
   17 | | Duplicate titles/status/instruction text crowded play | UX | Compact counters, color-based turns, local Hammer/Water playfield rotation and inverse keypad input |
   18 | 
   19 | ## Verification and limits
   20 | 
   21 | Targeted rules tests cover precision, ties/sudden death, duplicate stops/resolution, invalid input, pause timing, seeded AI replay and difficulty differences. Browser tests cover an entire five-round Water match, rotated keypad coordinates, AI delay, Timer pause/resume and Hammer's six-strike result flow. Full regression results are recorded in EXPANSION_COMPLETION.md.
   22 | 
   23 | No changes to core scoring or tournament attempt-token logic. These games report standard results once. Active precision-game attempts restart after process closure; completed tournament rounds remain persisted. This is a known checkpoint limitation, not a claim of mid-round restoration. No physical Android/iOS verification or long-duration heap soak.
   24 | 
   25 | ## Additional Golf integration findings
   26 | 
   27 | The later Golf route table used raw XOR low bits to select variants; correlated seeds and roles collapsed Medium onto one route. Selection now uses the existing avalanche seed mixer. Once both attempt records exist, AIChallengeMode now completes immediately; finish-time tolerance remains in winner comparison. Existing newer stroke-first competitive scoring was preserved. Four deterministic legal tee-to-cup fixtures and the three added route/competition regressions pass. Alternative navigation waypoint variants have not all been proved to finish autonomously.
~~~

## docs/ARCHITECTURE.md
SHA-256: b8b027dffa214f966c5d4d70645624f958f3582d0fe0156289c2d28fe0d0d7b3
~~~text
    1 | # Architecture
    2 | 
    3 | Pocket Rivals has one persistent Phaser instance and one reusable host scene. The DOM owns scrolling menus and accessible modal controls; Phaser owns gameplay and its HUD. Default logical coordinates are 420×760, fitted to the viewport and rendered at up to 2× device resolution. Modules may declare responsive custom presentation (Golf), own accessible DOM controls, and receive viewport resize notifications.
    4 | 
    5 | | Area                                                        | Responsibility                                                                         |
    6 | | ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
    7 | | `core/GameRegistry`, `GameLoader`                           | Eager metadata discovery; lazy module factories from both game roots                   |
    8 | | `core/GameManager`                                          | Navigation, foreground/background lifecycle, current-run guards, native back button    |
    9 | | `scenes/GameHost`                                           | Module context, monotonic elapsed time, HUD, initialization/shutdown generation guards |
   10 | | `core/InputManager`                                         | Pointer ownership, scene-local taps/drags/keys, cancellation and cleanup               |
   11 | | `core/TournamentManager`                                    | Serializable state machine, attempt tokens, checkpoints and one-time scoring           |
   12 | | `tournament/TournamentScene`                                | Metadata-driven setup, progress, champion and rematch UI                               |
   13 | | `core/StorageManager`, `ScoreManager`, `ArcadeScoreManager` | Validated local data, session fallback, separate duel and arcade scoring               |
   14 | | `core/AudioManager`                                         | Small procedural Web Audio effects, persisted preferences                              |
   15 | | `shared/contracts`                                          | Module, result and AI contracts; no game-specific rules                                |
   16 | | `shared/physics`, `rules`, `utilities`                      | Fixed-step accumulator, stable motion, match clock, cancellable worker tasks           |
   17 | | `games/*`, `arcade/*`                                       | Independently maintained rules, rendering, AI, assets, metadata and state              |
   18 | 
   19 | ## Lifecycle and navigation
   20 | 
   21 | `menu → loading → playing ↔ paused → results`. Every launch receives a new run ID. Shutdown disposes the previous module and input manager. A stale import or worker result cannot update a newer match. An opaque themed transition covers loading; the canvas is revealed after the first completed render. Menu cards never begin at zero opacity. Modal updates preserve the existing panel rather than replaying the entrance animation.
   22 | 
   23 | The host computes elapsed seconds using `performance.now()`, resetting its reference on resume. Physics accumulators cap catch-up at 100 ms; Pong/Hockey match clocks receive uncapped foreground elapsed time and persist through goals. Backgrounding pauses modules and clears held controls. There is no secondary RAF loop.
   24 | 
   25 | ## Module boundaries
   26 | 
   27 | `config.ts` imports only contract types and a small local preview. `index.ts` exports a side-effect-free factory. A module initializes only after selection; code remains in the browser's module cache after exit, while scene objects, inputs, timers and workers are released. Future texture-based modules must remove their own uniquely prefixed textures on disposal.
   28 | 
   29 | Game-specific work stays inside its folder. Pong retains registration ID `ping-pong` for saved-data compatibility. Tic-Tac-Toe lazily loads Classic or Ultimate through one metadata entry. Arcade declares `category: 'arcade'` and `tournament: false`; its result path never changes rival wins or tournament points.
   30 | 
   31 | ## Persistence and tournaments
   32 | 
   33 | - `pocket-rivals.v1`: existing sound/music and overall duel scores; retained without migration.
   34 | - `pocket-rivals.match.v1`: most recent unfinished quick match. Board games save legal move histories. Pong/Hockey save clocks and physics about once per second and on pause. Arcade games do not expose duel resume checkpoints.
   35 | - `pocket-rivals.tournament.v1`: plan, completed results, points, attempt identity and current module checkpoint.
   36 | - `pocket-rivals.ultimate-golf.v1`: four validated course best scores; active golf courses restart after closure.
   37 | - `pocket-rivals.arcade.v1`: per-game high scores. Arcade runs themselves restart after closure.
   38 | 
   39 | Tournament states are `between → playing → between/complete`. A token combines tournament ID, round index and attempt number. Restart creates a new attempt; duplicate/stale results cannot score. Wins give one point; draws give half to each. Rematches retain the schedule with a new tournament ID. Registry metadata, not game names, controls participation.
   40 | 
   41 | ## AI and performance
   42 | 
   43 | Pong/Hockey use predictive decisions plus an acceleration-limited movement controller. Classic uses alpha-beta Minimax. Ultimate and Connect Four use bounded iterative deepening, move ordering and transposition tables in workers. Workers terminate on pause/exit and have a two-second watchdog. Difficulty affects search/reaction/accuracy, never rule exemptions.
   44 | 
   45 | Star Patrol separates wave definitions, power-up data, combat simulation and vector rendering inside its lazy module. It reserves 52 player/28 enemy projectile slots, eight falling pickups and 24 short effects. Gear and enemy attacks use the same fixed-step clock; no extra loops or timers. Scene graphics are retained. Additional games add metadata/thumbnail bytes to the shell, but their implementation and worker chunks stay lazy. The built-in Phaser runtime remains the dominant shared payload.
   46 | 
   47 | Ultimate Golf uses a 240 Hz shared simulation and responsive, uniformly scaled portrait/landscape camera with exact inverse pointer transforms. Its `modes/` controllers isolate casual records, seeded hot-seat races and real worker-planned AI races. Physics, data, rendering and input remain shared under `games/mini-golf/ultimate`; the registry ID is unchanged. It has its own single/multi-course competition and remains excluded from global duel tournaments.
   48 | 
   49 | Development-only `?diagnostics` displays FPS, smoothed frame time, initialization times, active scenes, texture count, heap where available, AI search time and loaded module IDs. `window.__POCKET__` exposes read-only development snapshots for automated tests. Neither diagnostic UI nor snapshot access is enabled in production.
   50 | 
   51 | ## Web and Android
   52 | 
   53 | Vite builds static relative URLs, suitable for Vercel (`vercel.json`) and Capacitor's local origin. Web service-worker installation caches the shell only. Selected game chunks cache on demand; Settings → Save all games offline explicitly caches the full build, including worker files. Android always packages every registered module and asset and bypasses the web service worker. No network permission or runtime server is required.
   54 | 
   55 | ## Expanded rivalry collection
   56 | 
   57 | Three active expansion modules remain isolated under `games/`. They run a bounded 120Hz simulation through FixedStep and use ordinary duel results and metadata-driven tournament eligibility. Flappy Jump, Car Duel, Archery Duel and Chicken Jump are preserved under `src/future-games/`, outside the registry/loader globs; their code, assets and tests remain available for future development. Spike Attacks uses a small visibility graph on wave changes, not a worker or a continuously recomputed route. New real-time matches restart after process closure; existing board/Pong/Hockey checkpoints are unchanged.
   58 | 
   59 | Water Guess and Perfect Timer retain separate rule engines and renderers. Round resolution is idempotent. Perfect Timer uses a module-local foreground monotonic clock for both keyboard/touch stops and AI; pause time is excluded. Both use seeded match personalities, with no forced minimum error at Impossible.
   60 | 
   61 | TurnView is a small lazy presentation utility used by full-field local hot-seat games. It rotates only module-owned display objects, supplies the inverse pointer mapping, blocks interaction through its 280ms transition, and destroys its children on disposal. Host navigation remains fixed. Turn-based boards use pastel player backgrounds and compact neutral status; simultaneous games retain their separate controls.
   62 | 
   63 | Gravity Runner and Happy Birds interpolate fixed-step presentation separately from physics. Gravity streams bounded seeded obstacle sections, with runnable middle rails across double-wall gaps, four map-specific trap families and staged increasing run speed; it has no time deadline. Its CourseStream selects weighted nonperiodic motifs and retires old geometry. Canonical convex geometry and timed jet/gate states are shared by rendering, collision and all three AI forecasts. Happy Birds uses one shared wall-bounce arena with telegraphed safe pattern changes, a first-to-15 physical star goal and individual three-second animated returns to center after a collision. It has no match deadline; recovery freezes on pause and never awards or removes stars. Local Happy Birds controls are Space for Orange and arrow keys for Blue.
   64 | 
   65 | Spike Attacks uses a shared square arena, three solid cover blocks and four piston lanes per edge. Its module owns bounded attack phases, a visibility-route AI, interpolated presentation and two host-managed joystick drags. Foreground deadline is two minutes; game-specific physics and controls stay within its module.
~~~

All seven declare tournament compatibility and report the existing result contract. One host scene, no new frameworks, no network services and no added dependencies. Each module has cleanup and terminal guards. Car's per-pointer button adapter explicitly removes its own scene/canvas subscriptions.

Compared with the recorded AI-pass build, the shell grew about 2.7KB compressed as the seven games and concurrent metadata changes were integrated. Their implementation and AI code remain outside the initial static import graph.

    1 | # Gravity Runner / Happy Birds refinement

    1 | # Happy Birds: star race and animated recovery
    2 | 
    3 | First to 15 actual star pickups wins. One shared gold star replaces the old survival point system; nearest contact earns the pickup, while exactly simultaneous equal contacts share it. Equal same-step finishes draw. There is no two-minute deadline. Collisions retain every collected star and never award an opponent a point.
    4 | 
    5 | Each collision starts that bird's own three-second recovery. The bird turns gray, eases along a curved path toward the middle, gradually regains its player color, then automatically flies again. Collision and collection are disabled while recovering; the other bird continues normally. No countdown number, cooldown bar or timer label appears. Pause and background handling freeze the animation and rules together.
    6 | 
    7 | Recovery.ts contains timing, easing and color interpolation; Stars.ts owns seeded placement and swept pickup checks. Positions now range across the open arena instead of two fixed side slots, avoiding active birds and the previous location. The menu illustration uses only the birds and a star, with no surrounding frame. Both stay inside the lazily loaded game module. Existing keyboard/touch controls remain. AI now targets visible stars as well as safe wall openings, using the same physics and flap restrictions. Lightweight star bursts, a thumbnail star and compact star-goal markers provide feedback without extra panels.
    8 | 
    9 | The initial star-race milestone passed 287 unit tests: all three difficulties complete 100 seeded real star races apiece; precise three-second recovery, independent opponent play, no collection during recovery, no duplicate scoring, terminal state, ties, spawn reproducibility and frame-rate consistency are covered. All 19 focused browser checks passed across the initial run and corrected reruns. They exercise gray/partial/full color stages, return motion, pause, input rejection during recovery, cleanup, touch controls and real tournament scoring. The Vite production build and lazy-bundle check are also run. Desktop Chrome/touch emulation is not physical Android testing.
   10 | 
   11 | Single-star refinement: exactly one collectible is active until the winning pickup. Seeded random positions span the open arena, reject nearby repeats and avoid active birds. The simplified preview has no nested frame. All 15 targeted unit checks and seven focused browser checks pass, including 300 seeded AI races with the new spawn logic; production build and lazy-bundle checks pass.

## docs/PRIVACY.md
SHA-256: 711ff1a774c76768189c3c494d4badd0f6ef9b7732de8e1c0d0410cf54c4c3a1
~~~text
    1 | # Pocket Rivals privacy and data handling
    2 | 
    3 | Draft for publication, 2026-10-13. Add your publisher identity, contact email, and effective release date before hosting this as the public privacy policy.
    4 | 
    5 | Pocket Rivals is an offline collection for solo play or two people sharing one device. It does not create accounts, collect personal information, send analytics or crash reports, track users, show advertising, offer purchases, or contact a backend. Game artwork, fonts, code and sound synthesis are packaged locally.
    6 | 
    7 | The app saves sound/music preferences, overall duel wins/draws, tournament plans and results, arcade high scores, and unfinished game checkpoints in local app storage. Board checkpoints contain legal move histories; physical games contain positions and clocks. These records never leave the device. Names, contact details, location and device identifiers are not collected. Native Android cloud backup is disabled. Use Settings → Reset the scoreboard to erase scores, or clear app data/uninstall to erase all preferences and local data.
    8 | 
    9 | In the browser version, a service worker stores the application files in the browser's cache as they are played, or through the explicit Save all games offline option. Browser storage/site-data controls can remove these files. If hosted later, the hosting provider may process ordinary request logs; review that hosting arrangement and update this policy before publication. There is currently no hosted public deployment.
   10 | 
   11 | No app permissions are requested. Google Play or Android may independently process data under their own policies; Pocket Rivals contains no SDK to receive or transmit that information.
   12 | 
   13 | The game offers no social messaging, uploads, user-generated content or external game links. Review the Play target-audience and family policy requirements when selecting the final audience; no regulatory certification is claimed here.
   14 | 
   15 | Suggested Data safety basis: no data collected or shared by this app as implemented. The publisher must verify the release binary, dependency set and any later integrations before submitting the final declaration.
   16 | 
   17 | Ultimate Golf stores four local course records under `pocket-rivals.ultimate-golf.v1`. No player names or reference-game score files are imported.
~~~

Ultimate covers routing, all resolved-board cases, global outcomes and saved-history validation. Connect Four covers all 69 winning windows and bounded tactical AI. Snake and Shooter cover collision/scoring/projectile and wave lifecycle rules.
   18 | 
   19 | Ultimate Golf uses four full legal Easy-mode tee-to-cup shot replays: Foundry 15, Shoreline 15, Event Horizon 13, Lost Temple 11. No position resets or hazard bypasses are used in those replays. Additional tests check every course's final-stroke capture, exhausted strokes, high-speed thin walls, embedded/rotating colliders, 30/60/120 FPS consistency, tides/current, portals, UFO carrying, bridge regeneration, pressure doors, quicksand and 90 simulated seconds per course/difficulty. Browser checks exercise real mouse and CDP touch gestures at desktop, 320×568 mobile and landscape viewport sizes.
   20 | 
   21 | Lost Temple was also completed through real CDP browser touch gestures in 14 strokes with no hazard recovery; its actual victory overlay, Finish run result and persisted course record were checked. Clock control accelerated elapsed time without modifying positions, scores or game state.
   22 | 
   23 | Visual screenshots were inspected for the menu, board games, Arcade and golf course picker/overview/focus. The course viewport is exactly 288×512 (9:16), rotated from the original map without changing physical distances. No current game objects/listeners remain after host shutdown.
   24 | 
   25 | ## Measured performance
   26 | 
   27 | `node scripts/measure-performance.mjs` sampled each golf course for three seconds after warmup in headless desktop Chrome, development build, 412×915 mobile viewport, DPR 1. Samples were approximately 59.95–60.04 FPS and 16.6–16.7 ms/frame; golf initialization was approximately 30 ms. One active scene, 11 shared textures and 25 scene children remained stable. Full samples and heap measurements are in `performance-report.json`. These measurements are neither a mobile-device guarantee nor a production hardware benchmark.
   28 | 
   29 | Only lightweight metadata and SVG thumbnails enter the initial shell. Golf's simulation/rendering/course data is a separate lazy chunk; the old golf worker is no longer shipped. Web shell caching is automatic; full offline caching is explicit in Settings. The offline browser test disables networking before reloading and exercising all registered games and the board-game workers.
   30 | 
   31 | ## Remaining verification / limits
   32 | 
   33 | - Install JDK 21 and Android SDK 36, rebuild the APK, and test real multi-touch, lifecycle/back navigation, cutouts, audio latency and sustained performance on representative phones.
   34 | - iOS Safari and lower-end Android GPUs have not been physically tested. Landscape browsers letterbox the portrait board.
   35 | - Ultimate/Connect Four Impossible are bounded strong searches, not mathematical guarantees. Golf is intentionally solo; source difficulty controls hazards, not an AI opponent.
   36 | - Golf course records persist; an unfinished golf course restarts after closure. Its former duel source is retained but no longer registered. Old golf tournament rounds need a new tournament; other game state remains compatible.
   37 | - Full golf routes were demonstrated on Easy; Normal/Hard physics were stress-tested, not exhaustively solved.
   38 | - Named-player reference score files and original C art/audio are not imported. Source provenance and adaptations are documented in `ULTIMATE_GOLF.md`.

## docs/SPIKE_ATTACKS_REFINEMENT.md
SHA-256: 2e887e78bbe25a278eef0598aa1482a75367b94d602f02dcc9efba072f061c39
~~~text
    1 | # Spike Attacks — 16 October 2026
    2 | 
    3 | The supplied [reference short](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/p1eZhSl-U_g) was viewed in the in-app browser, including frames around 18%, 36%, 69% and 83%. It shows two players in one tiled square arena, three solid cover blocks, four wide piston spikes per edge, warning lamps and extending/retracting attacks. The previous prototype's separate arenas, circular stones and projectile rain did not match that composition.
    4 | 
    5 | ## Changes
    6 | 
    7 | - One shared square arena, three physical cover blocks and original Pocket Rivals vector characters. Both players have the same hazards, movement limits and collision rules; avatars do not push each other.
    8 | - Four physical piston lanes per edge. Each shaft stops at its first block. Circle/shaft/triangle contact uses the same dimensions as drawing. Bounded 120Hz checks and conservative swept extension prevent tunnelling.
    9 | - Seeded warning, extension, hold, eased return and recovery phases. Consecutive attacks change edges, preventing repeated-side camping. Warnings ramp from 1.85s to a 1.05s minimum, extension speed increases from 620 to 940 world units/s and hold time grows modestly. Cover and narrow gaps remain legitimate escape options.
   10 | - Two independently owned joysticks, mouse drag support and keyboard alternatives in How to Play. Release, cancellation and pause clear movement. A presentation layer interpolates movement/shafts and smooths facing without writing physics.
   11 | - Clean warning lamps replace central instructions. Existing procedural audio supplies strike, impact, return, collision and round feedback. First five survival points; simultaneous deaths replay. An independent 120-second foreground deadline preserves the lead or draws tied scores and excludes pause/background time.
   12 | - Bounded AI plans routes around the actual blocks, ranks comparable legal safe positions using its seeded profile, and uses the same movement speed as humans. Medium/Hard/Impossible reaction delays differ; no teleportation, fabricated scores or arbitrary deaths.
   13 | 
   14 | Archery Duel and Chicken Jump were moved intact into `src/future-games/`, alongside Flappy Jump and Car Duel. Their source, assets, metadata, IDs and module instructions remain. Unit tests still run; inactive browser specs are retained individually in `tests/future/`. They are absent from menu/tournament discovery and production bundles. Restore a folder to `src/games/` to reactivate it. No Math Quiz module, shared navigation or tournament code was changed.
   15 | 
   16 | ## Verification
   17 | 
   18 | - Full suite: **260 unit tests passed**. Spike coverage includes tip/shaft contacts and block shielding, bounded sliding/no tunnelling, single scoring and simultaneous deaths, actual return to sockets, progressive difficulty, safe reachable routes on every edge, 100 seeded 40-second strongest-AI traversals, 100 reaction samples per difficulty, interpolation isolation, deadline and terminal guards. Fixed-step outcomes match at 30/60/120 render FPS.
   19 | - **12 browser scenarios passed**, including simultaneous joystick touches, pause/cancellation, mouse input, repeated entry/exit, a complete real AI match, two-minute deadline, 360×640 layout, deferred-game exclusion, tournament scoring and Gravity/Happy Birds regressions. Start, strike and small-screen screenshots were inspected.
   20 | - Production Vite/TypeScript build, initial-payload budget and automatic new-folder discovery check pass. The production manifest contains 18 lazy games and no deferred games.
   21 | - Short headless desktop Chrome samples at a touch viewport measured ~60 FPS, ~16.7ms frames, ~1ms AI planning, a stable 11 scene children and zero host input listeners after exit. `expansion-performance.json` records the samples. These are short desktop measurements, not Android hardware or long-session certification.
   22 | 
   23 | No physical Android testing, external asset reuse, deployment or publishing occurred. Device touch feel and speaker playback still warrant real-device verification.
   24 | 
   25 | ## Local preview and controls follow-up
   26 | 
   27 | The development server runs at http://127.0.0.1:5173/. Solo keyboard controls accept either arrows or WASD; local two-player retains independent WASD/arrow controls. Both on-screen joysticks remain usable. Standard gamepads use the left stick or D-pad, first connected controller for Orange and second for local Blue. Browsers may require pressing a controller button before exposing it. Dead zones ignore drift, disconnects preserve the other player’s slot, and pause blocks held gamepad motion until neutral. Input is polled within the existing loop with no added listeners or dependency.
   28 | 
   29 | Controls verification: 10 targeted unit checks and five browser scenarios passed, including solo arrows, simultaneous local keyboards, touch/mouse controls, simulated browser gamepad input, dead-zone/assignment behavior and neutral gating after pause. Production build and bundle budget pass. No physical gamepad or Android-device test was performed.
   30 | 
   31 | ## AI collision and maps follow-up
   32 | 
   33 | The old 60-unit shafts left 20-unit gaps around a diameter-18 player. AI could park at lane intersections forever. Shafts now share a 72-unit visible/physical width, closing that loophole for everyone. All three data-driven maps have reachable cover on each edge and are checked for permanent four-direction safe spots. Exposed AI takes the exact same lethal hit as a human; no score manipulation or forced misses. Medium uses slower shelter-center decisions while Hard/Impossible evaluate tighter legal routes.
   34 | 
   35 | Courtyard, Split Steps and Crosswind are selectable through standard game variants, with a reproducible Random choice. Rendering, collision, spawning and AI all use the selected map. Existing IDs and old unspecified-map matches retain Courtyard. Only human joysticks are drawn: solo shows Orange, local shows both. Solo accepts WASD/arrows; local keeps WASD for Orange and arrows for Blue.
   36 | 
   37 | Validation of the follow-up: the full 276-test unit suite passed, including 100 seeded mixed-difficulty Spike matches across all maps, genuine lethal AI collisions, all-edge reachability, no permanent safe camping point and difficulty timing. Eight browser checks passed for maps, hidden AI controls, local/solo keyboard, mouse/touch, simulated gamepads, complete AI matches and tournament regression. Map previews derive from the same map data; mobile checks confirm all four choices and no horizontal overflow. Initial implementation remains lazy and within the 24KB gzip shell budget.
